body_markdown:
Every year, the Hagerty Media and Automotive Intelligence valuation teams gather and have spirited discussions to select the cars for the next Bull Market List. Together, we pore over trends and data to pick which cars we think will rise in value over the coming year. *(Stay tuned—the 2027 Bull Market List is coming in early December—Ed.)* As one of the data analysts responsible for suggesting Bull Market candidates, I have seen worthy cars get left on the cutting-room floor.


Some that didn’t make the cut often reemerge in the slide deck of possibilities for the next year, where they either make the list or get tossed out again. Their failure to make the cut isn’t so much that the data doesn’t support them; rather, they have to clear a wide range of hurdles—some objective, some subjective—before becoming a selection. Here are a few reasons why good picks (and some bad picks) fail to make the final Bull Market List.


## Too Tough to Find


### **2000–06 Honda Insight**


Honda


At risk of immediately losing my credibility, I’m going to address this choice first. Yes, the Honda Insight is a hybrid. Yes, it only has 73 combined horsepower. But the Insight was not your typical hybrid, and it’s got a surprisingly strong enthusiast following.


Unlike the rival Prius, which strived to be a normal sedan with great gas mileage, the original Honda Insight sacrificed practicality for efficiency. Forget about rear seats; to maximize aerodynamics, Honda gave the Insight a 4.3-inch narrower rear track to accentuate its teardrop shape, resulting in a 0.25 coefficient of drag. To achieve a sub-1900-pound curb weight, the Insight’s aluminum body panels were welded to its rigid aluminum monocoque structure, with many of the suspension and braking components, as well as the wheels, constructed of aluminum to reduce unsprung weight. Since it used aluminum so extensively, it was built alongside the[NSX](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=acura+nsx) and[S2000](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=honda+s2000) at Honda’s Suzuka factory. Like those classic sports cars, it also had an optional five-speed manual.


Honda


From a data perspective, it checks all the boxes—young enthusiasts make up two-thirds of its buyers, and millennials insure them for 21% more than any other group. The Insight’s average insured value increased 35% in recent years, but at $7700 it’s still affordable, and most importantly, they are rare. Maybe too rare. With only 14,000 sold in the U.S., combined with 20 years of attrition and almost no parts support (this is particularly critical for the Insight, given its batteries), finding an original Honda Insight to drive and photograph became our white whale.


It was not to be. At the end of the day, the Bull Market List needs to be cars that enthusiasts can actively shop for, and if we had considerable difficulty sourcing a suitable one within a 200-mile radius of our shoot location, with all of Hagerty’s resources at our disposal, recommending people go out and find one seemed unreasonable.


### **2001–05 Renault Clio V6**


Renault


This one might take less convincing. A spiritual successor to the[Renault R5 Turbo](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/renault/r5/1983/1983-renault-r5-turbo_1?id=aCn1I000000D0LsSAK) , the Clio V6 used the same formula—take a front-engine, front-wheel-drive economy car, rip out the rear seats, move the engine behind the driver, double the power and send it to the rear wheels.


All this re-engineering added 660 pounds over the sportiest regular Clio, but with a 3.0-liter V-6 that topped out at 255 horsepower in its Phase II form, the mid-engined Clio V6 could sprint to 60 in under 6 seconds and reach a top speed of 153 mph. The Clio V6’s wide body and functional side ducts look every bit as wild as the car drives.


Renault only made about 2800 of these hot hatches and didn’t sell any of them in the U.S. They just became legal to import this year. The Clio may well be on its way to increased values, but it didn’t make the cut for the story given its scant availability in the U.S.


## Picked a Similar Car with Better Stats


### **2006–08 Audi RS4**


Audi


The B7-generation Audi RS4 had everything it needed to be a good Bull Market pick—limited production, special powertrain, and love from younger collectors who are buying the best examples. So, what can beat a timeless all-wheel-drive German sedan with a 420-horsepower 4.2-liter naturally aspirated 8000 rpm V-8? Another sports sedan.


In a given year, we try not to fill the list with similar cars. Had we ignored that guideline, the 2018 list would have been 10 Japanese sports cars. While the RS4 had a 45% millennial quote share, millennials made up 58% of the quotes for the car we did pick for the 2027 list, and that car also had a higher pipeline gap (the percentage of quotes from millennials or younger collectors vs. their share of policies). In the end, the data led us to a stronger choice, so we tabled the RS4.


### **1997 **–** 2000 Mercedes-Benz C43 AMG**


Mercedes-Benz


The[C43 AMG](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/mercedes~benz/c43/1999/1999-mercedes~benz-c43-amg?id=aCn1I000000CsBpSAK) offers astounding performance for the money. For under $20K, you could have a compact sedan with a 302-horsepower 4.3-liter V-8 that could reach 60 miles per hour in just 5.7 seconds. All data pointed to the C43 being a good Bull Market pick. Quote count and average value were growing five times faster than the Hagerty average, 55% of quotes were from collectors under 40, and average Hagerty Price Guide values were rising and pulling away from the C36. However, it lost out last year to the E60-generation BMW M5—yep,[the one with the V-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=F4-RPcSGVFI) . At the end of the day, the[M5](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/bmw/m5/2009/2009-bmw-m5-base?id=aCn1I000000DGNdSAO) just had more compelling data, which is what this whole exercise is about, and proved to be the better pick.


With a year of data between when we made that choice and now, we see that our call was on the money: The average #2 value for the C43 rose 21%, while the E60 M5 rose 34%.


### **1965 ****–**** 76 Lancia Fulvia**


Broad Arrow


Some of the most beautiful cars ever made came out of Italy in the 1960s, but few have ever made our Bull Market List. Last year, two candidates in this segment emerged—the[1967 – 72 Alfa Romeo 1750 GTV](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=alfa+romeo+1750+gtv) and the[Lancia Fulvia](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=lancia+fulvia) . The GTV won out, being the more notable classic, though the Fulvia had solid numbers. A year out from that ruling, neither pick proved to be strong, as average #2-condition values for both dropped 3% last year.


## Cars that Might be Too Niche


### **1990 ******–****** 94 Nissan Pulsar GTI-R**


Nissan


Homologation rally cars are always cool, and this Nissan is no exception. Built to compete in Group A Rally, the Pulsar GTI-R is powered by a 227-horsepower turbocharged 2.0-liter four-cylinder that sends power to all four wheels through an ATTESA system similar to the Skyline GT-R’s, while only weighing 2400 pounds. Nissan made just over 14,000 of these, so they are rare enough to be collectible, and they aren’t impossible to find. Also, consider that Nissan never made a newer, quicker generation of this the Pulsar GTI-R—a factor that puts downward pressure on Skyline R32 and R33 values.


Pulsars are extremely popular with young enthusiasts (nearly a quarter of quotes come from Gen Z). The car’s demographics actually skew a little younger than those of the R32 Skyline, and Pulsar values have been steadily on the rise since they became legal to import. So why did it never make our list? A variety of reasons.


We’ve considered the Pulsar GTI-R many times. I floated it so ofted that it became a bit of an inside joke. Some years we thought it was still too obscure. Others, it lost out to some other right-hand-drive JDM vehicle. One time, I campaigned for the Suzuki Cappuccino over the Pulsar. The Suzuku’s data was good, and it offered a fun counterbalance to the Hummer H1 (also in the[2023 Bull Market List](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/bull-market-2023/) ). The pictures did not disappoint, and the Cappuccino saw the same value growth that year as the Pulsar (+5%).[The next year](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/bull-market-2024/) , we had the same dilemma: choose between the Pulsar GTI-R and the Mitsubishi Pajero Evo. We opted for the Pajero Evo, which had just become legal to import; it seemed more of the moment.


In this case, the Pulsar GTI-R would have been the better pick, besting the Pajero Evo by 8 points (4% growth vs 12%). While I gave up pitching the Pulsar, it *might* still be a good pick. Since 2022, the average #2 value has risen 48%. And from my perspective they seem like a deal again, compared with the rest of the market: #2-condition values are still below $30,000.


### **1999 ******–****** 2001 Isuzu VehiCross**


Isuzu


I have a reputation for loving esoteric (and often terrible) cars, and I have argued (and would again) that the VehiCross is secretly great. Isuzu built the VehiCross more or less as a prototype to showcase the company’s off-road technology, including aluminum monotube shocks with external expansion chambers and a high-tech torque-on-demand system that uses 12 independent sensors to send power to the wheels with the most traction.


Rarity is often a factor in collectibility, but usually not for Isuzu’s reasons. To speed up development and reduce costs, at the expense of tooling longevity, Isuzu used ceramic tooling dies instead of steel to stamp the oddly-shaped body panels. Fewer than 6000 were produced before the dies wore out.


Values for Japanese trucks and SUVs have exploded over the last decade, with the VehiCross mostly left out of the action. The highest recorded sale is only $26,647, for the[last VehiCross ever built](https://carsandbids.com/auctions/rJDnAopE/2001-isuzu-vehicross) , with most between $10K and $15K. If this had a Toyota badge, I think it’d be worth five times more.
